analysis.one_liner: Lets investors sue brokers and companies in court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: Introduced by six Democratic senators, the bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned brokers, dealers, and investment advisers from writing contracts that force customers to settle disputes in private arbitration, accept a pre-picked forum, or give up the right to join a class action. It would also have barred public companies from forcing shareholders into arbitration in their bylaws or shareholder agreements. Investors who prefer arbitration could still choose it once a dispute actually arises.
analysis.who_benefits: Retail investors with brokerage or advisory accounts, and shareholders of public companies. Anyone defrauded by a broker or adviser could take the firm to court or join a class action, instead of being funneled into an arbitration system the firm selected in the fine print before any dispute existed. Existing forced-arbitration and class-waiver clauses would be voided going forward.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for brokers, dealers, funding portals, and municipal securities dealers to write customer agreements that mandate arbitration, lock in a chosen forum, or bar customers from suing individually or as a class.
Applies the same ban to investment advisers, so advisory clients keep the option of going to court.
Bars public companies from mandating arbitration in their bylaws, governing documents, or shareholder contracts, and lets the SEC refuse to register securities from issuers that impose such mandates.
Voids forced-arbitration and class-waiver provisions in agreements already in effect, while leaving arbitrations that had already started untouched.
Keeps arbitration available as a genuine choice: nothing stops an investor from selecting arbitration after a dispute arises if they judge it the better forum.

analysis.who_pays: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and public companies, which would face lawsuits in court — including class actions — and lose the automatic advantage of pre-dispute arbitration clauses they wrote themselves. Some of those added legal costs could reach customers as higher fees, since the bill sets no limits on that.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration through the industry's FINRA forum is often faster and cheaper for a small individual claim than a court case; the bill removes the guaranteed arbitration track for small investors unless they affirmatively choose it after a dispute.

Re-enabling class actions exposes firms to large settlements in which class members can receive small individual payments while attorneys' fees are substantial, which is the industry's core objection to class-action waivers being voided.

Firms facing more court litigation would bear higher dispute-resolution costs and could pass some of them to customers through higher fees or reduced services; the bill contains no offsetting protection against that.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — restoring defrauded investors' access to court and to class actions when firms have taken both away by contract — is real but indirect, and the main costs fall on financial firms rather than the public, though some could reach customers as fees. The strongest objection, that arbitration is quicker and cheaper for small claims, is softened by the bill's design: arbitration stays available to any investor who wants it, it just can no longer be forced on them before a dispute exists.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on December 5, 2019, joined by five Democratic colleagues: Durbin, Blumenthal, Warren, Menendez, and Whitehouse.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and public companies, which keep the forced-arbitration and class-action-waiver clauses the bill would have voided; defrauded investors are left with the same limited recourse they had before.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban mandatory pre-dispute arbitration in investor agreements.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral on December 5, 2019 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there.

against.name: Securities industry trade groups
against.what_they_did: Have long defended mandatory pre-dispute arbitration in customer agreements as faster and cheaper, and opposed legislative bans on the practice.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-chaired Banking Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: Nearly all retail brokerage customer agreements require arbitration and waive class actions; the bill would void those clauses and expose firms to court suits, including class actions, over fraud claims.
Advisory agreements with the same forced-arbitration and class-waiver terms would become unlawful, ending the advisers' pre-selected private forum for client disputes.
Companies could no longer adopt bylaws or shareholder contracts mandating arbitration of shareholder disputes, and the SEC could refuse to register their securities if they tried.
The guaranteed stream of mandatory arbitration cases would end, but the forum remains fully available to any investor who chooses it after a dispute arises.
Class-action and individual fraud suits in court that current waivers block would reopen, expanding the market for lawyers who represent investors.
